sections.title: Lesson 8.1: Calculating Yields and Returns
sections.overview: Yield measures investment income as a percentage of the investment's cost or current market value. This lesson covers current yield (also called dividend yield for stocks), capital gains and losses generated from closing positions, and total return — which combines income with realized or unrealized gains and losses. All yield figures on the SIE are annualized.
key_concepts: Current Yield (CY) applies to both stocks and bonds; when applied to a stock dividend it is called dividend yield.
CY is always an ANNUAL figure — quarterly dividends must be multiplied by 4 before dividing by market price.
Preferred stock dividend yield: take the stated rate × $100 par to get annual dividend, then divide by current market price.
Capital gain/loss is realized only when a position is CLOSED (sold for a long position, bought back for a short).
Adjusted cost basis = original purchase price modified by corporate actions such as stock splits or stock dividends.
Total return blends income (dividends/interest) AND capital gain or loss, expressed as a percentage of cost basis.
Total return may use realized gains/losses on closed positions OR unrealized gains/losses on open positions.
Unrealized gains/losses on open positions have no tax impact but DO count for total return.
rules: Quarterly dividends must be annualized (× 4) before computing current/dividend yield.
Cost basis must be adjusted for stock splits and stock dividends before computing gain or loss (e.g., 4:1 split reduces per-share basis to one-fourth).
formulas: Current Yield (Dividend Yield) = annual income (dollars) / current market price
Capital Gain or Loss = sales proceeds − adjusted cost basis
Adjusted Cost Basis (after stock split) = original cost basis / split ratio
Total Return = (income + capital gain or − capital loss) / cost basis
Total Return % = Total Return $ ÷ cost basis × 100
mnemonics: "TR = IGC": Income + Gains ÷ Cost basis = Total Return.

sections.title: Lesson 8.2: Taxation
sections.overview: Ordinary income is the combination of earned, investment (portfolio), and passive income, and it determines an investor's marginal tax rate. Capital gains are split between short-term (≤1 year, taxed as ordinary income) and long-term (>1 year, taxed at preferential 0%/15%/20% rates). This lesson also covers offsetting losses against gains, the $3,000 ordinary-income offset with indefinite carryforward, and the 30-day wash sale rule.
key_concepts: Ordinary Income = Earned Income + Investment (Portfolio) Income + Passive Income + Short-Term Capital Gains.
Earned Income: salary, wages, bonuses, tips, self-employment income — only earned income qualifies for IRA contributions.
Investment/Portfolio Income: dividends and interest from securities held.
Passive Income: from DPPs (limited partnerships) and certain real estate; passive LOSSES may offset ONLY passive income.
Short-Term Capital Gain: position held one year or less — taxed as ordinary income.
Long-Term Capital Gain: position held MORE THAN one year — taxed at preferential 0%, 15%, or 20% rates (brackets indexed annually).
Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) of 3.8% applies to investment income above MAGI thresholds, on top of capital gains rates.
Qualified Dividends are taxed at long-term capital gains rates IF the investor held the underlying common stock more than 60 days within the 121-day window surrounding the ex-dividend date.
Capital losses offset capital gains dollar-for-dollar; excess losses may offset up to $3,000 of ordinary income per year.
Unused capital losses carry forward INDEFINITELY (no time limit) to future tax years.
Unrealized gains/losses on open positions have NO tax consequences.
Wash Sale Rule: a loss is DISALLOWED if the investor buys back the same or substantially identical security within 30 days BEFORE or AFTER the sale (61-day window total).
Disallowed wash-sale loss is added to the cost basis of the replacement security (not lost — deferred).
Substantially identical securities include call options, rights, warrants, and convertible securities (bonds or preferred) of the same issuer that convert/exercise into the same common stock.
Wash sale rule applies to recreating SHORT positions as well as long positions.
A wash sale itself is not illegal; claiming the disallowed loss is.
rules: IRC long-term holding period: MORE than one year (a position held exactly one year is short term).
$3,000 maximum annual offset of net capital losses against ordinary income.
Capital loss carryforward: indefinite, no expiration.
Wash sale window: 30 days before + day of sale + 30 days after = 61 days; disallowed loss is added to basis of replacement shares and holding period tacks on.
LTCG tax brackets: 0% / 15% / 20% (income-thresholds adjusted annually for inflation).
Net Investment Income Tax: additional 3.8% on net investment income above MAGI thresholds.
Qualified dividend holding period: > 60 days within the 121-day period beginning 60 days before the ex-dividend date.
Passive losses may only offset passive income — never earned or portfolio income.
formulas: Ordinary Income = Earned + Portfolio (Interest & Dividends) + Passive + Short-Term Gains
Net Capital Gain/Loss = Total Capital Gains − Total Capital Losses
Maximum Ordinary Income Offset from Net Losses = $3,000 per year
Carryforward Loss = Net Capital Loss − $3,000 (carried indefinitely to future years)
Replacement Cost Basis after Wash Sale = Purchase Price of Replacement + Disallowed Loss
mnemonics: "E-I-P-S" feeds Ordinary Income: Earned, Investment, Passive, Short-term gains.
"Passive offsets Passive" — losses from DPPs stay in their own bucket.
"More than a year for the lower tier" — LTCG requires holding > 1 year.
"30 before, 30 after — Wash!" — 61-day wash sale window.
"3K and Carry" — $3,000 ordinary-income offset, rest carries forward indefinitely.
Qualified dividend: "60 in 121" — held >60 days within the 121-day window.
